question. Whats a good source of protein on a vegan diet?

Tofu and beans are both fantastic. The fact that they're both quite cheap is one big point in their favor right from the start. If you have an Asian market near you than you can usually get really good prices on tofu. In my area at least the supermarkets are a bit of a gamble. Tofu might be reasonably priced, and it might be up to twice what I'd consider fair. And of course dried beans are incredibly cheap even if you factor in some spices or veggies to add in when cooking them.

They're both incredibly versatile too. Tofu starts out with a range of firmness. And the texture and taste are also easily changed further during the cooking phase. The same tofu block as part of a soup and part of a stir fry can almost seem like two different foods. It doesn't hurt that tofu's also a good source of calcium. I don't think calcium gets stressed nearly enough when people talk about vegan or even vegetarian diets. Especially given the continuing evidence about negative effects of calcium supplementation when compared with getting it from one's diet.

Beans are also up there when it comes to versatility. They soak up flavor wonderfully when you add some spices or vegetables to the pot when cooking them. Obviously they're great for any traditionally bean filled meal. But they're also fantastic as a basic pliable material to work with. It's only a couple more steps to take black beans and turn them into a black bean vegiburger, for example. I've heard a lot of arguments about the role of rice when it comes to eating beans for protein. From the best I could make of it the issue seems to be pretty overblown though, especially if rice is a heavy part of your diet anyway.

I wouldn't really put them at the same level as tofu or beans, but I think it's worth giving a nod to mushrooms too. Most people probably aren't going to want to eat enough to get a huge protein boost. But I find them to be a great way of adding a bit more....I guess I'd say meatiness to the texture of a meal without using actual meat. It's something like 0.5 grams of protein per cap while only giving an additional 5 calories or so. I usually go with white mushrooms if I'm looking for another flavor sponge type addition and shiitake if I'm looking for actual flavor to come with it. The latter also provide a lot more in the way of a general nutritional boost in comparison to standard white mushrooms. I usually just go with dried and re-hydrate as needed. If eating plain I'd always go with fresh. But as long as they're being cooked anyway I don't think dried mushrooms have all that much lower quality in taste when compared to fresh. Again, Asian markets can be great for that. Dried shiitake in standard supermarkets are overpriced well into the ripoff level. Even going with amazon will usually give a lot better price there. And in general "fresh" shiitake in standard grocery stores are anything but.

It can seem boring at first when protein gets pushed into only a couple staples. But the real trick is finding ways to change those two items into a much wider variety of tastes.

Not to mention, even if you did eat more packaged foods, they would still generate tons more garbage just based on volume. I've been eating a lot of frozen food lately, like these quinoa veggie burgers. They come 4 to a box. I eat 1 box a week. So that's 1 carboard box and 4 cellophane bags. Say a fatty ate quinoa burgers, they would probably eat a box a day along with everything else they eat.
No they need a product with high content of MSG , high fructose corn syrup and sodium to want to eat it.

Another good reason to go raw, less garbage and dishes. I eat a lot of fruits and vegetables and eggs, so I only have to deal with a cutting board, knife, cast iron, and some tupperware. Let's just say I haven't had to clean my sink out in quite some time.

We get free food from work a lot and it comes in take out boxes, but they are biodegradable so they can go in the green bins. I get leftover salads from work meetings and I use my Tupperware. It's always the salad that no one eats.
Being sensible with food has its perks.
